This document is the northstar: where SchemaBot is going and why. It is deliberately not a
description of shipped behavior. [invariants.md](./invariants.md) is the registry of what is true
today and where it is enforced, [engines.md](./engines.md) is the capability matrix, and
[postgresql.md](./postgresql.md) is the current PostgreSQL envelope. When this document and those
disagree, those are right and this one is a statement of intent.

The separation matters. The invariants registry is only useful if every entry describes behavior
that actually holds, so aspiration needs somewhere else to live. This is that place.

## The northstar

Every database that someone cares about should be able to evolve safely, whether it is a weekend
project or a tier-zero fleet, and whoever is making the change should not have to become a database
expert to do it without breaking something.

That second half is the part that has changed. For most of the history of this problem, the person
writing a schema change was a person, and the industry's answer was to make them more careful:
review checklists, runbooks, a database team who says no. Increasingly the author is an agent, and
"be more careful" does not generalize to something that will write a thousand changes a week
without getting tired or getting better. Nor is there usually just one of them. The guardrails, and
the coordination between authors, both have to move into the tool.

## Four properties

### From a vibe-coded experiment to a tier-zero database

The same tool should serve both ends of that range.

Today they are served by different worlds. Someone building a side project uses whatever their
framework bundles and finds out at deploy time whether it worked. A large organization staffs a
platform team, builds an internal pipeline, and gates changes behind humans. The interesting thing
is that both make the same class of mistake: a change that locks a table, a drop nobody intended, a
half-applied state nobody can name. Scale changes the blast radius, not the failure mode.

Safety here comes from the plan and the gates, not from the size of the deployment running them.
The diff against the live database, the lint, the destructive-change acknowledgment, the refusal to
call an ambiguous result a success: none of those need a platform team to be correct. So there is no
principled reason the hobbyist gets the unsafe version.

What has to become true is that the cost of adoption collapses at the small end without weakening
anything at the large end. A tier-zero fleet wants the control plane: a server, durable state, lease
ownership, an operator who can stop a change that is running. An experiment wants none of that and
should not pay for it. The same engine, the same gates, two very different amounts of scaffolding
around them.

### GitOps, not GitHub

The source of truth is the schema in version control, and the loop that reconciles it against the
live database. GitHub is the best-supported interface to that loop. It is not the substrate, and
SchemaBot should never quietly become a tool that only works if you happen to use it.

This is the pillar that is furthest along, because it is already enforced rather than intended:

- **AV-1** states it directly: GitHub is an interface to SchemaBot, not a dependency of it. CLI and
  API applies work when GitHub is down, and a data plane never needs a GitHub App at all.
- **AV-10** is the half that makes AV-1 useful: anything the PR can do, the CLI can do. Plan, apply,
  the destructive-change confirmation, stop, start, cancel, cutover, revert, skip-revert, release,
  rollback, unlock. A fallback that covers most of the surface is not a fallback.
- **MG-9** closes the failure mode where an outage becomes an invention: GitHub being down never
  makes SchemaBot guess at state.

The direction of travel is to keep widening that gap between the model and the interface. Every
feature should be asked the AV-10 question before it ships: if this only works through a PR comment,
it is not finished. A forge other than GitHub, a CI system, a terminal, or an agent calling an API
should all be able to drive the same loop, because none of them are where the truth lives.

### Guardrails and context for agents

Agents are bad at imperative change scripts and good at declarative desired state, and that is not a
stylistic observation. Writing a correct `ALTER` requires knowing the current state of the database,
the ordering against every other pending change, and how to undo it. Editing a `CREATE TABLE` file
requires none of that, because the diff engine derives all three. Declarative schema is what makes
agent-authored schema change tractable at all.

That earns SchemaBot the right to be the tool agents reach for, and it creates two obligations.

**Context.** An agent should be able to see the schema as readable files, ask what a proposed change
would actually do against the live database, and get an answer specific enough to act on: this
rewrites the table, this holds a lock for the duration, this is refused on this engine and here is
why. Today most of that exists but is shaped for a person reading a PR comment. It should be
equally available to something that is not reading.

**Guardrails that do not care who wrote the change.** This is the load-bearing one. The gates are
author-agnostic by construction: **RV-1** applies what was reviewed, **RV-3** requires explicit and
re-checked consent for destructive changes, **MG-1** never converts uncertainty into a passing
check, **AZ-2** fails closed at every tier. None of them ask whether a human or an agent produced
the DDL, and none of them should ever start asking. An agent that can talk its way past a gate is a
gate that was never real.

The honest framing is that SchemaBot does not make agents trustworthy. It makes the question
irrelevant, by ensuring the change is checked the same way regardless of the answer.

### Many agents, one database

A single agent writing a schema change is the easy case. The real shape of agentic development is a
swarm: several agents building one feature, or several features at once, several of which need the
same database to change. The hard problem stops being "is this DDL correct" and becomes "what
happens when three of them are right at the same time".

This is a coordination problem, and coordination is not something each agent can solve on its own.
An agent can be careful about its own change. It cannot know that another agent, in another process,
planned against the same table forty seconds ago and is about to apply. Nothing an individual author
does makes that safe. It has to be enforced somewhere both of them are forced to go through, and for
schema changes that place is SchemaBot.

The primitives for this already exist, because concurrency was never optional. SchemaBot has always
had to survive several pods, several operators, and redelivered webhooks racing each other:

- **OW-5** allows one active apply per deployment. Two changes to the same database cannot interleave,
  no matter how many authors produced them.
- **OW-1**, **OW-2**, and **OW-6** make ownership explicit and provable: every drive runs under a
  claim, writes are scoped to a lease token, and there is exactly one way to acquire work. A second
  actor cannot half-take a change that someone else is driving.
- **RV-2** is the multiplayer race stated as a rule: a plan built against a schema that has since
  moved never applies. The agent that planned first does not win by being first to submit.
- The merge gate is already an agent-to-agent protocol, without either agent knowing it. When one
  change lands, every other open pull request whose files no longer match the live schema goes red.
  The second agent is told to reconcile, by the same mechanism that would have told a person.

That last point is the one worth internalizing, because it is the cheap version of a problem people
usually try to solve with a scheduler. Agents do not need to negotiate with each other, discover
each other, or agree on an ordering. They need a shared source of truth and a gate that fails closed
when their view of it is stale. Both already exist.

What the swarm case still needs is legibility. Serialization is correct today but opaque: an agent
whose change is queued behind another cannot see the queue, cannot tell whether it is waiting on
something that will finish in seconds or in three weeks, and gets a red check that explains the
problem in prose written for a human. Coordination that works but cannot be reasoned about forces
agents into polling and retries, which is how a swarm turns a correct system into a thundering one.
The direction is to make the ordering, the reason for a block, and the expected wait into things a
caller can read and act on.

## What does not change

A vision that quietly weakens the invariants is not a vision, it is a rewrite. Three things hold
regardless of how far any of the above gets:

- **Uncertainty fails closed.** Storage that will not answer, an ambiguous ownership claim, an
  engine state nobody recognizes: all of these block. None of them pass.
- **The operator is never surprised.** No change runs that was not planned and consented to, and a
  change that has started stays authoritative until someone resolves it.
- **A narrower engine is not a looser one.** Adding a database or a deployment shape never comes at
  the cost of the guarantees. If a capability cannot be delivered safely on an engine, the answer is
  a refusal at plan time, not a quieter gate.

## What this document is not

- **Not a roadmap.** There are no dates here and no commitments to ship any particular thing. It
  describes a direction so that individual decisions can be checked against it.
- **Not a description of current behavior.** Read [invariants.md](./invariants.md) and
  [engines.md](./engines.md) for that, and believe the badges in the README over anything written
  here.
- **Not an argument for supporting everything.** Breadth that costs safety is not progress. The
  range in the first property is about deployment size, not about saying yes to every database.

## Where we are today

| Property | What already holds | What is missing |
|---|---|---|
| Experiment to tier zero | The gates and the plan are the same at any scale. Local mode drives a database from a DSN with no data plane. | The small end still pays for the large end: a server, storage, and a GitHub App for the PR flow. PostgreSQL, the likeliest engine at that end, is early alpha. |
| GitOps, not GitHub | AV-1, AV-10, and MG-9 are enforced. A data plane carries no GitHub credentials. | The merge gate itself is expressed as GitHub Check Runs. No second forge is implemented, so the separation is proven by the CLI rather than by a second integration. |
| Agents | Declarative files are already an agent-readable source of truth, and every gate is author-agnostic. | No dedicated agent surface. An agent works by reading files and opening a PR, the same as a person, with none of the plan detail available programmatically. |
| Many agents, one database | Concurrent authors are already serialized and made safe by OW-5, OW-1, OW-2, OW-6, and RV-2. The merge gate coordinates open changes with no protocol between them. | The coordination is opaque. There is no readable queue, no machine-readable reason for a block, and no expected wait, so a blocked caller can only poll. |
